hints: Focus on the two different trends you need to test at once, how first ionisation energy changes across Period 3 and how melting point depends on structure and bonding.
Remember the two famous dips in first ionisation energy across Period 3, from Mg down to Al and from P down to S, due to sub-shell stability.
Compare giant structures with very high melting points to simple molecular structures with very low melting points, then check which middle element is highest for ionisation but lowest for melting.
walkthrough:
**Recall the first ionisation energy trend**

Think of first ionisation energy as how hard it is to remove the outer electron. Across Period 3 it generally increases because nuclear charge increases.

But there are two dips: $\text{Mg} > \text{Al}$ because the $3p$ electron in Al is easier to remove than the full $3s^2$ in Mg, and $\text{P} > \text{S}$ because P has a stable half-filled $3p^3$ arrangement.

**Recall the melting point trend**

Think about structure, not just position. Giant metallic and giant covalent structures melt very high, simple molecular structures melt very low.

In Period 3: $\text{Na, Mg, Al, Si}$ are giant with high melting points rising to Si, then $\text{P, S, Cl, Ar}$ are simple molecules with very low melting points.

**Test element R in each set**

For R to fit, it must be the highest ionisation energy of its trio AND the lowest melting point of its trio.

Only $\text{P}$ in the trio $\text{Si, P, S}$ fits both: $\text{P} > \text{S} > \text{Si}$ for first ionisation energy, and $\text{P}$ ($\text{P}_4$ molecules) melts lower than giant $\text{Si}$ and $\text{S}_8$.

**Confirm the identities**

Q, R and S are consecutive, so if R is phosphorus, Q must be the element before it and S the element after it.

That gives $\text{Q} = \text{Si}$, $\text{R} = \text{P}$, $\text{S} = \text{S}$.

options.A: R = Mg does have the highest first ionisation energy of Na, Mg, Al because Mg > Al > Na. However Mg does not have the lowest melting point. Na is a soft metal with weak metallic bonding and melts at about 98 C, much lower than Mg at about 650 C. This option traps students who only check ionisation energy.
options.B: R = Al fails on ionisation energy. The order is Si > Mg > Al, so Si has the highest, not Al. This is due to the dip from Mg (full 3s2) to Al (one 3p electron). It also fails on melting point because Mg and Si both melt higher than Al is not the lowest in a simple way. Students who forget the Mg to Al dip choose this.
options.C: R = Si fails on both tests. For ionisation energy, P > Si > Al, so P is highest, not Si. For melting point, Si is giant covalent with a huge melting point near 1410 C, so it is the highest of the three, not the lowest. P as a simple P4 molecule is much lower. This traps students who think ionisation energy rises smoothly with no dips.
options.D: R = P is correct on both counts. For ionisation energy, P > S > Si because P has the stable half-filled 3p3 configuration, so P is highest. For melting point, Si is giant covalent (very high), S is S8 molecules and P is P4 molecules, with P melting lower than S. So P is the lowest. Hence Q = Si, R = P, S = S fits perfectly.
